assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum-model prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle, followed by correlated-insulator and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, opened a new field in which interaction strength is tuned by geometry. From an electronic-structure view this is a rare case where a relatively simple theory predicted a precise quantitative condition and experiment then confirmed it. The impact on correlated-electron physics is broad and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive theoretical prediction. Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the 2018 experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states. A three-way prize is natural and supported by the supplied names. Other experimental groups (for example Dean's) and the Cao first-author role are not in the credited names, so some allocation of credit remains unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups have reproduced the main phenomena and the field is mature in under a decade. The mechanism of superconductivity is still debated, but the discovery of flat-band correlated phases is stable and does not depend on it.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconducting phase is unresolved.
Sample-to-sample variability and twist-angle disorder complicate the interpretation of some states.
I have not independently verified which experimental credit the committee would treat as primary.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Car-Parrinello method unified density-functional electronic structure with molecular dynamics, allowing forces to be computed on the fly and enabling finite-temperature simulation of liquids, defects and chemical reactions without empirical potentials. It underlies a large part of modern computational condensed-matter and materials physics. The originality, clarity and breadth of impact are very high, and I recognise that this is close to my own field and weigh it with that in mind.
assessment.attribution: The 1985 paper by Car and Parrinello is a clean, two-person attribution with no real ambiguity. Others (Payne, Kresse and others) built related ab initio MD schemes later, but the credited pair made the foundational step.
assessment.maturity: Four decades of continuous use and independent reimplementation in many codes make this fully mature. If anything recognition is overdue, though it may be considered by some to sit near chemistry's remit.
uncertainties: The boundary with chemistry or computational methods in the physics prize scope may be contested.
Whether a method development should rank above a discovery for this year's physics prize is a committee judgement.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-type models with controllable parameters, observing the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic Mott states and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This provides an analogue simulator for the strongly correlated physics I study numerically. The importance and lasting impact on many-body physics are high.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, Bloch and Greiner demonstrated the Mott transition, and Esslinger led the fermionic Mott and Fermi-Hubbard work. Selecting Bloch, Zoller and Esslinger gives a balanced theory plus experiment split, but Greiner's early Mott and microscope contributions make this omission a real attribution cost.
assessment.maturity: Experiments have been reproduced worldwide. The Nobel recognition of cold-atom cooling (1997) and condensation (2001) makes this a natural next step. Quantitative simulation beyond what classical methods can do is still emerging.
uncertainties: Four credited names and at most three can be selected; Greiner's omission is a genuine fairness concern.
Whether analogue simulators have yet solved an open problem that classical computation could not.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Kane-Mele proposal of the quantum spin Hall effect, the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction and the HgTe observation by Molenkamp's group established topological band insulators, a classification of electronic phases that is central to contemporary condensed-matter physics. The concept is deeply linked to electronic-structure calculation (band inversion, spin-orbit coupling) and is lasting.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the theoretical foundation; Molenkamp's group delivered the experimental realisation. The supplied credit omits Bernevig, Zhang and others (for example Fu and Kane for 3D), so this three-name prize would leave a contested allocation.
assessment.maturity: Many materials were confirmed independently by ARPES and transport, and the field has been stable for well over a decade. The 2016 prize already honoured topological phase transitions, which makes some committee members consider this partly recognised.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize and with other topological work may reduce urgency.
Credit for the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D topological insulator discovery is not represented in the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstration of record accuracy and stability, redefined precision timekeeping and provides a route to a redefinition of the second and to tests of fundamental physics. The idea is clear, original and concrete in its impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori invented the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and Ye brought it to the 10^-18 regime, giving a clean two-person configuration. Hall and Hansch were honoured in 2005 for frequency combs, so the credited pair is well separated from earlier prizes.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs have reproduced clocks at the 10^-18 level, and international comparisons are underway. The formal redefinition of the second has not yet occurred, so some consider the practical impact still maturing.
uncertainties: Contributions of other lattice-clock groups (for example Ludlow, Hinkley, Campbell) are not in the credited names.
Date of the SI second redefinition is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and the Ekert entanglement-based protocol founded quantum cryptography, and secure key distribution over fibre and satellite links has now been demonstrated. The conceptual originality is high and the link to practical technology is clear. This is more computer-science-like than my own field, so I weigh it modestly.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard authored BB84, and Ekert separately proposed the E91 entanglement-based protocol; this is a plausible three-way prize using all supplied names, with Ekert's independence of BB84 being a recognised point of attribution discussion.
assessment.maturity: Experimental QKD is established, though the deployed security versus device imperfections remains a research topic. The 2022 prize on entanglement experiments partly prepared the recognition of this area.
uncertainties: Practical security of real devices is not fully settled.
Whether the committee treats this as physics rather than information science.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought strong light-matter coupling into superconducting circuits, enabling dispersive readout and the scalable architecture used in today's quantum processors. Impact on the quantum-technology field is major and the idea is clear.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theoretical proposal by Blais, Girvin and colleagues and the experimental realisation by Wallraff and Schoelkopf are the decisive steps. Wallraff is not among the supplied names, which weakens fairness of the proposed configuration. I propose the three supplied names as the only available option.
assessment.maturity: The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits by Clarke, Devoret and Martinis overlaps in subject and may reduce near-term appetite. Reproduction across many labs is complete, but technology is still evolving.
uncertainties: Recent prize in an adjacent area and the omission of Wallraff and Devoret complicate attribution.
Timeliness is debatable because processors are not yet at a stage of decisive application.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of superconductivity in LaFeAsO(1-x)Fx at 26 K and the rapid rise of Tc beyond 50 K established a second family of high-temperature superconductors with a complex multiband, magnetically proximate electronic structure. It is a notable discovery for materials physics and a stimulating testing ground for electronic-structure and magnetic-fluctuation theory.
assessment.attribution: Hosono's group made the original discovery, while Chen and Zhao led groups reported higher Tc in related compounds soon after. The first-discovery credit is clear but the priority of later Tc improvements is of lesser conceptual weight.
assessment.maturity: The discovery is robustly confirmed, but the pairing mechanism remains unsettled and the family has not reached practical application. Recognition is feasible but the field has not delivered a decisive unifying picture.
uncertainties: Whether subsequent Tc records merit equal credit to the original discovery.
Possible perception that cuprates (already recognised in 1987) overshadow this.
